source_text:
Εὐσταθίου Ἀντιοχείας ἐξ ἑρμηνείας τοῦ ιεʹ ψαλμοῦ· Ἐξαπέστειλεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν υἱὸν αὐτοῦ γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικός· οὐ γενομένους, ἀλλὰ γενόμενον· μοναδικὸν γὰρ τὸ πρόσωπον· οὐκ εἶπον μοναδικὴν τὴν φύσιν·
ἄπαγε, μὴ γένοιτο· οὐδὲ τὴν αὐτὴν οὐσίαν σαρκὸς καὶ θεότητος, ἀλλ' εἶπον ἕνα Κύριον Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν, δι' οὗ τὰ πάντα, ἐν τῷ διαφόρῳ τῶν φύσεων, γνωριζόμενον κατὰ πάντα.
orientation: Eustathius is closing his interpretation of Psalm 15 by quoting Galatians 4:4 and explaining that the singular 'born' points to Christ's one person, not one nature.
pass_a_gloss: Of Eustathius of Antioch, from the interpretation of the fifteenth psalm: God sent his Son, born of a woman; not 'born ones,' but 'born'; for the person is singular; I did not say the nature is singular; away with it, may it not be; nor the same substance of flesh and divinity, but I said one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, known in the difference of the natures, in all things.

choices.why: Glossary term; preserves the passive sense of γίνομαι with ἐκ for origin.
Keeps the predicate adjective force of μοναδικόν and the article with πρόσωπον.

choices.english: away with it, may it not be
choices.why: Renders the strong rejection idiom literally, preserving both the interjection and the optative wish.

choices.english: in the difference of the natures
choices.why: Literal rendering of the articular infinitive-like noun phrase; keeps the dative of sphere.
Preserves the passive participle and the distributive κατὰ πάντα.

bible_refs.note: Ἐξαπέστειλεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν υἱὸν αὐτοῦ γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικός

pass_b_english: From Eustathius of Antioch, from his interpretation of Psalm 15: “God sent his Son, born of a woman” (Galatians 4:4). I did not say “born ones,” but “born,” for the person is singular. I did not say the nature is singular—away with it, may it not be! Nor did I say that flesh and divinity have the same substance. Rather, I said one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, known in all things in the difference of the natures.

problems.quote: He did not say "born ones," but "born," for the person is singular. I did not say the nature is singular
problems.source_quote: οὐ γενομένους, ἀλλὰ γενόμενον· μοναδικὸν γὰρ τὸ πρόσωπον· οὐκ εἶπον μοναδικὴν τὴν φύσιν
problems.why: Eustathius speaks in first person throughout; English shifts to third person 'He did not say' then first person 'I did not say', confusing speaker.
problems.fix: I did not say 'born ones,' but 'born,' for the person is singular. I did not say the nature is singular
problems.ruling: Source has no explicit subject; οὐ γενομένους ἀλλὰ γενόμενον is Eustathius quoting/paraphrasing Paul, so 'He did not say' is defensible, not an error.
